DR SANDIE BOHIN (continued)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Good morning, Dr Bohin. Is it all right if the witness --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, please, do sit down. Obviously you're still subject to the oath that you took.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Bohin, I would like, if we may, please, to move to the case of [Baby B]. You have written one substantive report on [Baby B] dated 17 March 2019; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Now, turning to -- first to the material that you were asked to look at. It's set out in paragraph 4.3 of your report, which is about halfway down or two-thirds of the way down the second page.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Were you given a copy of [Baby B]'s medical notes from the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Copies of the X-rays or radiographs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the witness statement from Dr Evans of 31 May 2018?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So in other words not his initial sift report, but his final, in inverted commas, report?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And were you also given a couple of photographs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I was.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And can you just explain, just remind us, please, what your role was so far as your instructions are concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was asked to peer review the report of Dr Dewi Evans and I was asked to review case notes of babies, in this particular case [Baby B], and to ascertain, on the evidence contained within the case notes and the information I was given, if I could find a cause for her collapse.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm not going to ask you to explain this every time you return to give evidence, and I'm well aware you have told the jury once, but just to remind the jury please on this occasion, what is peer review?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's reviewing what someone else has done before you.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So it means looking at what others have done. It doesn't mean completely reviewing things from the start, but of course you do have to, in a clinical context, look at the case notes. But it means to review what someone else has done before you, a colleague, someone of the same sort of standing as yourself.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: When you say "in a clinical context", most of us use clinical in the sense of cold-blooded. What does clinical mean in the way you use the word?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Forgive me. Clinical, my term, is something that is in a medical context, so looking at medical notes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, all right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You set out in your report [Baby B]'s background which in essence is a summary of her life in hospital; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It is. Dr Evans had already written in great detail about her -- the early part of her life, so I just wrote what I thought were the salient points.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. And you record as a matter of fact the circumstances surrounding [Baby B]'s collapse. I'm now looking at paragraph 6.8 of your report.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That was, just to remind the jury, at 00.33 in the early hours of 10 June.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You then set out further details from the notes, and you came to an opinion at section 7 of your report which is at the bottom of page 5 of 7; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far as the time between [Baby B]'s birth, just after 8 pm on the 7th, and her collapse at just after 00.30 on 10 June, what conclusion from the notes did you reach as to her clinical state?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: At birth she was clearly compromised and needed some help to establish normal -- a normal breathing pattern.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So she did need resuscitation at birth, and that would not be particularly unusual for a baby born at just after 31 weeks' gestation. But she responded very well to appropriate resuscitation provided by the medical and nursing team.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thereafter she needed some respiratory support in the form of either BiPAP or CPAP, and again that would be the kind of respiratory support that you would expect a baby of that gestation to need.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But she stabilised very quickly after the initial resuscitation and was stable -- she was initially put on BiPAP, which is a specific form of CPAP, it is CPAP with a little bit of extra support, but she did very well on that. So she was then converted to CPAP, but was in air, and her blood gases were normal. She was in air.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: She was very, very stable. Stable enough, in fact, to have times off CPAP, having skin-to-skin contact with her mother, and also for feeds to be started.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In terms of the time -- the duration of the time that she was off CPAP, I think we've made reference to the duration of that in paragraph 7.1. On your assessment of the notes that were being made at the time, what -- was this a case of [Baby B] coming off for 10 minutes or what?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In this particular case [Baby B] was taken off for 2 hours. There isn't a standard protocol for how long you would take babies off CPAP, but as Dr Evans said yesterday, in order to keep babies on CPAP, they have a kind of special hat and a bonnet with Velcro ties. So to get them on and off CPAP is a bit of an ordeal. So you wouldn't take a baby off for just 10 minutes, because that would be too much handling for little benefit.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In this case [Baby B] was taken on, on the first occasion, for 2 hours, and then was electively put back on. That was the plan.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: On the second time she was out for almost two and a half hours, and was having skin-to-skin contact with her mother. So that meant that she was very close to her mother's chest, and we know that has very positive benefits for both babies and mums.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is there any suggestion from the notes that that extended time without any breathing support at all was causing any distress to [Baby B] or compromising her in any way?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Certainly in the first 2 hours off, there was -- there were no hiccups at all. There was no change in her observations, so saturations, her respiratory range, her heart rate stayed the same.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The observations also remained the same during her second period off, but there is a documentation in the notes that she was put back on CPAP because of increased work of breathing, although
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: that isn't reflected in the observation chart because the observation chart just tells you the number of breaths per minute, it doesn't tell you if you're struggling to breathe or if the baby is compromised.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But there was nothing in the observation chart would suggest that she was compromised in any way.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Was it necessary to use oxygen that second time --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Oh, no, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. Having read the notes and having listened to the evidence surrounding the circumstances in which [Baby B] collapsed, are those circumstances that you have heard normal, in inverted commas?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. They are very concerning because babies of 31 weeks' gestation, although premature, you might anticipate that they might have some problems.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: [Baby B] -- the only problem [Baby B] had was that she was requiring some CPAP support. But despite being on CPAP, everything else was completely normal and stable, and so to suddenly collapse is not something that you see in babies of that gestation.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If they have a deterioration, you normally get some prior warning: maybe they don't tolerate their feed, they have some desaturations, they have some bradycardias, maybe. She had nothing that would suggest that she was suddenly going to collapse in this way.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So no warning signs at all.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There was, before the collapse at 00.33, a circumstance in which her nasal prongs became dislodged. Have you reached any views at all about that, that particular event?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nasal prongs can be misplaced. They usually fit quite snugly in the nose to form a seal in order to give the CPAP, but they can be misplaced. If that's the case, they're probably quite uncomfortable because they are not sitting in the nostril, they are sitting at the side of the nose and that can be uncomfortable.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If, over a period of time, they're left off, the baby may desaturate. But in this case it was noted, the prongs were replaced, and everything went back to normal.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And so far as you were concerned, in your professional opinion, is there any connection between the displacement of the nasal prongs and the desaturation at 00.33?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. None at all. There were no -- that was a kind of a mechanical problem. It was rectified and [Baby B] was fine. There were no other warning signs that would herald an imminent collapse.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And so considering the circumstances of the collapse, the nature of the collapse and the physical descriptions that you have heard given by the witnesses who saw the collapse or its immediate aftermath, what conclusion have you reached as to why [Baby B] collapsed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, on reviewing the evidence, I had to formulate what could possibly have caused this, and make a differential diagnosis, so a list of things that could possibly cause a baby to collapse, and then look at the evidence in front of me to see if any of those fitted with the way that [Baby B] collapsed, what she looked like when she collapsed, and how she subsequently recovered.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And so the usual things that you would expect in a premature baby, things like infection, could be discounted. Cardiac arrhythmias could be discounted because they just don't simply present in at that way.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So I was left with the conclusion that this was an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Was it simply that you had discounted all the other possibilities that led you to that conclusion or was there evidence that in itself in your view supported that as a conclusion?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, I think partly it was a diagnosis of exclusion, but the important thing was the very florid descriptions of this rash and the skin -- not a rash, the skin changes that were present during this.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Everybody that's commented on it has said how -- (a) how florid it was, how different it was from anything they'd ever seen before, and I know from researching the literature that this is found in cases of air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So it was the rash plus -- and the excluding other potential causes because it just didn't fit with any other known potential causes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In reaching your conclusion were you taking into account at all the circumstances surrounding the collapse of [Baby A]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I looked at this case on its own -- on its own -- on its own merit. But, you know -- and that is what I did for all the cases I have looked at. I have looked at this case on its own merits.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Bohin. Would you wait there, please, there will be some more questions for you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Of course.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Bohin, I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of Ms Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Some general questions first and then we are going to have a look at what you say about the two children you have reviewed.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: You began your professional career, in terms of special, as a paediatrician, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No, I was a neonatologist.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm not going to dispute you are a neonatologist. I wanted to confirm, if you began as a paediatrician and then became a neonatologist, that's all.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Junior doctor training, at that time, you trained as a neo -- trained as a paediatrician, but at that time you could also train and be accredited in neonatology, and I was accredited in paediatrics and neonatology, which was the only accreditation you could have at that time. Things are different now.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you've been a consult neonatologist during your professional life, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you'd agree, would you -- would you agree there's a difference between a neonatologist and a paediatrician?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, all paediatricians, as part of their training, then and now, have to undertake some neonatology as part of their training. So all junior doctors, whether they end up being a consultant paediatrician or a consultant neonatologist, have to undertake neonatal training at registrar level.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is there a difference between a consultant paediatrician and a consultant neonatologist?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There is in the neonatologist ends up working solely in neonatology, whereas a paediatrician may work in a smaller centre. Neonatologists work in tertiary centres and they don't work anywhere else.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Paediatricians work in smaller hospitals where they cover both neonates and paediatrics.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Neonatology is a specialised discipline, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Focusing on the first 4 weeks of life?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it focuses on longer than that, because babies who are born prematurely often stay in hospital for many months.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But a particular focus is that period after birth, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's the time from -- the time a baby is born until the time the baby is ready to leave a neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you think, in your professional expert opinion, Dr Bohin, that someone who spends a large part of their career working with neonates will recognise that subtle features can have a significant impact in their presentation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. It's not always obvious what's going to happen, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not to anyone.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No. Because if it was, deteriorations that are sudden and unexpected wouldn't happen at all, would they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, could you rephrase -- I don't understand the question, I'm sorry.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If it was obvious when something was going to happen, deteriorations that are significant could be stopped, they wouldn't get that far at all, would they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's not quite true because the majority of the time in neonates, you do get subtle changes and warnings before a baby
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: collapses. It's very unusual for a baby to go from being well to a collapse requiring resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Those changes can be quite subtle?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not always, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They can be, can't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They can be.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Do you agree that it's important for an expert, or someone who holds themselves out as an expert, to have current clinical experience?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not necessarily, no, because I think what you can't do is dispel the experience that a person may have had over many years. As long as they are current in their thinking and their reading, clinical practice -- and they are up to speed with clinical practice, the fact they are not doing day-to-day handson work, I think, makes little difference at all. In fact, lots of tertiary centre consultants don't do very much hands-on work, but that doesn't mean they are not credible.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you not regard it as important for an expert to be working in a current clinical environment in relation to a case that they are considering?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You don't think that's important?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't think it's crucial, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No. Are you -- do you think it's important for experts to develop their knowledge in clinical practice on an ongoing basis?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's the same thing, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I don't know. Do you think it's important? Sorry if it's a repetition?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you think experts can gain from colleague-to-colleague discussions about the babies they're dealing with day to day, and that enhances their knowledge?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's absolutely part of clinical practice that you discuss with your colleagues problems that you may have
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: encountered during your working day. But you also get that same sort of information by networking, going to conferences, and networking in that way. You talk.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What I asked you was: do you think it's important for them to have that type of contact with colleagues on the job, clinical contact?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's advantageous, but it's not essential.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It's advantageous.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You're aware that experts in court proceedings have particular duties, don't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Some of those are set out by the courts, that's correct, isn't it? And indeed the GMC, the General Medical Council, which regulates doctors who practise, that also has standards on expert evidence, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it does.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You're familiar with those?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I just want to ask you about a section in those rules called:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Acting as a witness in legal proceedings. Giving evidence as an expert witness."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You're familiar with that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. And maybe just -- I don't know if we can access D7, please. Perhaps at this point for Dr Bohin and for the -his Lordship and the lawyers.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just go over, please, to paragraph 12. Can we enlarge paragraph 12 so Dr Bohin can see this. I'm going to read out what paragraph 12 says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "You must only give expert testimony and opinions about issues that are within your professional competence or about which you have relevant knowledge including, for example, knowledge of the standards and nature of practice at the time of the incident or events that are the subject of the proceedings. If a particular question or issue falls outside your area of expertise, you should either refuse to answer or answer to the best of your
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: ability, but make it clear that you consider the matter to be outside your competence."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I only read the second bit for completeness.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Certainly the GMC, in their guidance to experts, regard it as important that someone holding themselves out as an expert should have knowledge of the standards and nature of practice at the time of the incident or events that are the subject of proceedings, don't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They do, but they don't say you need to be in clinical practice.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They said you should have knowledge of the standards and the nature of the practice?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That is enhanced by being in practice at that time, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, not necessarily, and it doesn't say that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Someone who is not in clinical practice will not have the same knowledge of the standards and nature of practice as somebody who is, will they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, they certainly can.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: How is -- just assist us with this: if somebody has retired from clinical practice in 2009 and is dealing with events that happened in 2015, do you say they are in the same position as someone who is in practice at that time?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If they have kept themselves up to date with clinical practice, then yes, absolutely.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If they have done that. In any event, your view, so I can make this quite clear, is that being in current clinical practice is no advantage to an expert; is that your view?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I didn't say that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is it of advantage to an expert then, if you didn't say that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It would be advantageous, but not essential, I think were the words I used.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Advantageous. Why?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because you are seeing day-to-day events, you're able to talk to peers. But you have still got a level of expertise that someone who is retired would have. They don't lose their expertise because they've retired.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So earlier I asked you if being in day-to-day practice and talking to peers was something that was significant and you disregarded that, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I didn't disregard it. I said it wasn't essential.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you accept in fact it is an advantage?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It could possibly be an advantage.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think, in fairness to the witness, she did say it was advantageous but not essential to have clinical contact with other practitioners at the time.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I apologise if I (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I think that's what you've just repeated essentially, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Peer review is not the same as approaching this as a kind of cold review, is it, if you see what I mean?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I can explain what I mean if you don't.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If you could, I would be grateful.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, of course. In peer review, your focus is looking on the work in this case that Dr Evans, in particular, has done, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It's not a case that you were handed all the papers and asked, absent whatever anybody else thinks, what do you think? It's not what has happened with you, is it, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it is. I was asked to peer-review Dr Evans' reports, but it was made very clear to me that I should form my own opinion about whether I agreed with Dr Evans' views, whether I disagreed with Dr Evans' views, or if I found an alternative explanation for why the children whose cases I reviewed collapsed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We can take this off the screen, by the way, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Bohin, I didn't mean to be rude when I said that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But by the time you came to look at the material in this case, you had a very clear idea what the allegations were, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I knew that there was a problem with babies collapsing at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Was it 2019 when you became involved with this?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's after the initial media reports and coverage of what had taken place at Chester, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So you had an idea of what this was about, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You were given Dr Evans' opinions via his reports, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Naturally. Did you have contact with Dr Evans?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Have you had contact with him over the course of these proceedings?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The first contact I had with Dr Evans was in -- I have never met Dr Evans before. The first contact I had with Dr Evans was earlier this year, in 2022, when we were asked to discuss a case -- one of the cases in this trial to formulate -- just to have a discussion about it because we had a difference of opinion. So that was the first time, and that was a telephone conversation because obviously I live in Guernsey, Dr Evans lives in the UK. I had never met him before.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Have any of your opinions been influenced by the mere fact of the allegation that is made rather than the facts relating to the case?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I took each case on its merits to try and -- looking at the evidence, to try and ascertain why each child collapsed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And are you able to give your opinions independently of Dr Evans, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, of course.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You've been provided with the witness statements in this case, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the medical exhibits?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And certainly, up to this point, you've been able to watch what has happened either in court or on the link, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I have.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Just before we turn to [Baby A], can I just ask, when, if ever, let me ask, did you last see a case of air embolus in your clinical practice?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So it may start off in a great vessel, but over time actually goes in further into the heart, and that can cause a problem.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: This long line had crossed the midline. It wasn't in that the heart. So if it went in further, it wouldn't have approached the heart, it would have just stayed in a vessel.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, we don't know where the tip of the long line ended up, do we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, in that very short spice of time, in a day, it wouldn't have moved. The recommendations are not to X-ray the tips of long lines every day. The recommendation -- there are recommendations about the care of long lines. There's a BAPM recommendation about the care of long lines because of the risk of cardiac tamponade. If the tip touches the heart, it can go through the heart muscle and cause a problem. So there are guidelines about that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But the recommendations are not to X-ray the tip of a long line every day.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Pause there, just go back to that. It's there if anyone wants to go to anything else.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: So if you will -- go ahead, Mr Myers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I didn't mean any discourtesy but in fact I was about to have a word with Mr Johnson along the lines your Lordship is about to speak to him, I think.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No.

blocks.text: It is merely a summary to highlight for them, basically, what was being said at the stage of interview?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
Yes, I'm sorry we are a few minutes late.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Mr Johnson?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Ladies and gentlemen, when I introduced the case to you a couple of weeks ago now, you will remember that I gave you an outline of each of the cases and I also told you, really probably in about 2 minutes, what Lucy Letby said in interview about each of the cases.

blocks.text: At the end of the evidence, when we've dealt with all the cases, you'll get the interviews in one go, but those will cover everything, and we have agreed between us that it may help you at this stage, while you have still got the evidence relating to [Baby A] and [Baby B] clear in your minds, it may help you to know what Lucy Letby said about it.

blocks.text: Summary of interview with Lucy Letby re [Baby A]
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (read)
Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So dealing with the case of [Baby A] first, the first interview took place on 4 July 2018. And Lucy Letby was given a chance to go through the relevant notes of [Baby A]'s treatment. And she was asked, and this is a direct quotation:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Do you specifically remember this shift with [Baby A]?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And she replied:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Yes."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said that the handover was at about 8 pm at his bedside in nursery 1. She said that the nurse caring for him, Melanie Taylor, was sterile and in the process of connecting or drawing up some fluids to connect via a long line that [Baby A] had had inserted during the day, and she recalled that the long line had been set up by the doctor.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby said that whilst she was receiving a handover from Nurse Taylor, she checked the fluids and that Nurse Taylor had connected them. She was asked this question:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "So did you retrieve that bag for [Baby A]?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And she replied:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Not that I recall. I recall that Mel already had the bag out."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Soon after we noticed that [Baby A] had gone pale and mottled in his skin."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "We called Dave Harkness over and initiated airway support as [Baby A] was apnoeic. A crash call was put out and Dr Jayaram attended."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said that full resuscitation attempts followed.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When asked about the handover, Lucy Letby described [Baby A] as:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "A little bit jittery in appearance and in his limbs."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She thought this may have been due to low blood sugar and she said he was due to have his blood gas and blood sugar levels checked shortly after she, that is Lucy Letby, came on shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She then said:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Mel was there with the fluids when I came to get handover and we made that a priority, to check the fluids, and got those set up and running."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The question was this:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Okay. And again, why was that? Was that a priority?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And she replied:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Because he hadn't had his cannula, his peripheral cannula, inserted in the day. He had a UVC that they weren't happy to use and he had a long line inserted that the doctors had confirmed we could use. So I think he'd gone a few hours without any fluids."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And question:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Okay, and is that normal? Is that a cause for concern?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She replied:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "It's not ideal, but when you have a new baby and it's -- you have -- you can have problems obtaining access to be able to give fluids."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She then said that the doctors had confirmed that the long line was ready to use and fluids were run. She said that [Baby A]'s colour changed and he became more pale after, she said, Nurse Taylor had connected the fluids.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She then said:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "It was fairly soon, within minutes, I think."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was asked:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Thirty minutes? Two minutes?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And replied:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "I don't know, maybe 5 minutes."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She remembered that she was at [Baby A]'s bedside checking equipment as it happened. She said that it was usual to receive
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: handover, and then check all emergency equipment at the cot side.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby said that Melanie Taylor remained in the room at this point. She couldn't remember what Nurse Taylor was doing, but thought that she may have been writing her notes. She said that Dr Harkness was in the room dealing with [Baby B] and said that Caroline Bennion was also in the room.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said the mottling she saw was:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "... blotchy, red and purple, almost a rash-like appearance."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Which Lucy Letby thought could be a sign of:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "... infection, low blood sugar, being cold or low blood gas."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It appeared on his hands and feet and it was to the left side of his body where his line was, but he was centrally pale.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was then asked this question:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Was it bright red? Was it dark red?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And she replied:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "I think he was more pale than the mottling, than the little areas of the mottling, but predominantly it was paleness."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And the question:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Did anyone else see that mottling on [Baby A]?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Her answer:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Yes. I think it was there when I called Dave, and Caroline and the other nursing staff came in."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then the question:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "And did they say anything about it to you?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Yes. We were advised to stop the fluids on the long line straight away."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby then said that when she went to [Baby A], she checked that the CPAP mask was still in place. She checked to see if the machine was running and if he was breathing. The machine was
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: still running and she found that he was apnoeic and not breathing.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby then said:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "And then, straight away, Dave was in the room.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Mel Taylor and I called him over from what I recall."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said that Mel Taylor and Caroline Bennion were still in the room and that:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "We were advised to stop the fluids on the long line straight away."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She couldn't -- Lucy Letby said that she couldn't recall [Baby A]'s resuscitation, but that at some stage Dr Jayaram attended the resuscitation which Dr Harkness had commenced. She said that [Baby A] then passed away.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby said it was awful and she agreed with the officer that it had been difficult for her. In terms of coping mechanisms, Lucy Letby said the team supported one another with it. She was asked who else she would have spoken to and couldn't specifically recall, but felt that she would have told her parents and her friends.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She couldn't remember if she'd passed [Baby A] to his parents after his death. She believed that mum's health problems were mentioned at the debrief held by Dr Jayaram and, when asked in interview, she thought it may have been a problem with either the line or the fluid attached to the line.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She couldn't recall for definite who had attached it, but believed it had been Melanie Taylor as she was sterile.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In considering the notes, she agreed that she'd completed [Baby A]'s handprints and footprints, with the consent of parents, for his memory box and had also taken a lock of his hair and the handprints and footprints of his sibling as the parents had wished.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said photographs were taken with the unit camera and the parents' phones, and she found the process quite a nice thing to do for the baby and the parents, as if it was a way of giving the parents memories.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said there was a bereavement checklist to go through when a baby had died, so the nurse would tick things that had been done such as handprints, footprints and photographs.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She discussed the nursing rota and shifts. She confirmed that she could often be called on a morning and asked to work overtime that night. On a week-to-week basis she could receive calls stating the unit was short of staff.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was asked further questions on 10 June 2019, moving on a year. She agreed that she had completed training on the administration of medications via long lines in May of 2015. She didn't think it contained anything specific on the risk of introducing air.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In November 2020, on 10 November 2020, she was interviewed again. She agreed that she'd been taught to prime lines so that they didn't have air in them and that it would be hard to push air into a line deliberately.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She denied having done so via either [Baby A]'s UVC or the long line, and she said that she didn't know exactly what an air embolus was. She had been taught to clear the line and make sure there wasn't any air in it as it could lead to an air embolism.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She had been trained how to avoid air embolism due to the danger they present and she was unaware of the physical effects of an air embolus and any changes to the appearance of the skin.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was questioned about Facebook and confirmed that she had an account at the time, which she'd access via her phone or a tablet. She explained that her relationship with the parents on the unit was only ever professional, either face to face in the unit or by telephone when necessary. She couldn't explain why she'd searched for [Baby A]'s mum, [Mother of Babies A & B], on three separate occasions in June 2015. She couldn't remember conducting the searches or why she'd done it.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When asked about a further search in September 2015, she thought she may have been looking for an update on [Baby B] as the nurses thought about babies on the unit and talked about them.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that's [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Summary of interview with Lucy Letby re [Baby B]
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: (read)
In relation to [Baby B], Lucy Letby was first interviewed about [Baby B] on 4 July 2018. She'd been given access to the notes of [Baby B]'s treatment.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She noted the administration of Babiven and lipids from 00.05 on 10 June 2015. She agreed she'd signed that entry, which ideally should have been co-signed.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She confirmed that [Nurse A ] was [Baby B]'s designated nurse.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said that she couldn't remember the shift with any clarity, but did remember [Baby B] displaying some mottling that looked a little bit similar to that seen on [Baby A] the day before. It was more extensive and covered more of her body in comparison rather than just the limbs like [Baby A]. [Baby B]'s was like a purply red patchy rash-like appearance.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby thought that [Nurse A ] may have alerted her to [Baby B]'s appearance, and Lucy Letby said that she was either in the room or at the nurses' station.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby B]'s appearance was observed before any resuscitation began. Lucy Letby said she couldn't recall if [Baby B] was attached to a monitor, but assumed she would have been. She didn't recall any alarm sounding. She said she didn't have any recollection of her interactions with [Baby B], nor did she recall having any concerns for [Baby B]. She couldn't remember in which room her designated baby was that night, but [Baby B] had been in nursery 1 and she would have attended to [Baby B] if [Baby B]'s designated nurse was on a break or engaged with another baby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She confirmed that if a nurse caring for that baby is doing something else, then a member of staff may do the drugs for the baby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She confirmed that she would have handled [Baby B] to an extent to give her medication and attach those lines.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was asked about connecting via a long line or a UVC, and this question was asked:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Does it need two people to do that?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She answered:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Yes."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And the question:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Because of the protocol or because physically you need two people?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She answered:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "So it's protocol that we would both go to the patient and connect it together."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said she'd taken the blood gas readings while another nurse would have been operating the Neopuff machine, and then the following exchange took place:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Question: At that time then do you remember how [Baby B] was, how she was presenting?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She responded:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "I don't recall at that time, but looking at this, it was happening during Neopuff, so she was obviously being Neopuffed by somebody while I was taking the blood gas."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The officer then said, "Right", and she said:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "And the blood gases aren't great, so..."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And the officer said:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Okay. So does that say to you that's post -- post-collapse?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She replied:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Or during, yes."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby said:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "The only concern primarily were the patients (sic)
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: and how they were coping with that. Obviously they'd already lost [Baby A], and then to have to see [Baby B] go through resuscitation."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She didn't recall how upset [Baby B]'s parents were and the following exchange took place. She said:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Just I know that they had waited a long time for [Baby A] and [Baby B], that they were much-wanted babies."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The officer asked:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Who told you that?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She replied:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Answer: It was known through the handover you have. So when you have a nursing handover you have a little bit of background as to the parents and the pregnancy and things."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Question: Does that sort change the way you deal with them or affect the way you deal with them?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Answer: No. I would like to think you treat all parents the same, but obviously you just bear in mind what we have they've gone through to get to that point.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But I think the care you would give them and their babies would be the same as any other parent."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So, my Lord, that's the summary at this stage, and there will be a lot more information in due course.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We are now going to move on to the case of [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, as my learned friend Mr Johnson just indicated, we are now going to move through the indictment to count 3 and the evidence in support of the allegation of murder in relation to [Baby C], who died on 14 June 2015. So we're moving from the events of the 8th to 11 June 2015 and to the days thereafter.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: But as your Lordship knows, and perhaps the jury ought to be informed, although we've substantially heard the evidence in relation to [Baby A] and [Baby B], for good logistical reasons, some expert evidence has been put back to later in the case. So we shall return to them in due course through the evidence of Professor Kinsey, the paediatric haematologist, and the pathologist, Dr Shukla and Dr Marnerides. But with those exceptions we will now move on to the case of [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Your Lordship should have a bundle of statements, about 26 pages in there. I'm grateful.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of [Mother of Baby C] (read)
Members of the jury, the first evidence in relation to this count to be placed before you comes in the statements of [Baby C]'s parents, which I'll now read to you.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The first statement is by his mother, [Mother of Baby C], dated 13 January 2019. And it reads:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I am [Mother of Baby C]. I provide this statement at the request of Cheshire Police. It gives a family history and
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: describes my experience of the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital and provides details of the tragic death of my son, [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I became pregnant to my husband [Father of Baby C] in early December 2014. This was my first pregnancy. At 20 weeks I went for an anatomy scan at the Countess of Chester Hospital. During the scan, the sonographer informed us that although everything appeared normal, the baby looked very small. At this point one of the foetal medicine midwives, named Julia, came in to see out. She explained she had liaised with one of the consultants, Sara Brigham, with regards to my pregnancy and it had been recommended that I had an amniocentesis to check if there were any genetic problems with my baby."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And the statement goes on to explain the nature of that test, and it's a test to check if a baby has any genetic or chromosomal conditions and involves the removal and testing of a small sample of cells from the, amniotic fluid.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Mother of Baby C]'s statement goes on:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I attended an appointment for an amniocentesis with the consultant Jim McCormack. Jim became my consultant from this point on and saw me through the remainder of my pregnancy.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was around 21 weeks pregnant when I had the amniocentesis. The results came back about a week later and showed there were no genetic problems with my baby.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: He was small but it was not known why.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "From this point on I underwent regular scans which were conducted by Jim McCormack. They were held approximately fortnightly. [Baby C] had growth scans and blood flow checks.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Around 28 weeks into the pregnancy things took a bit of a turn for the worse. [Baby C]'s growth began to falter and there were signs that the end of my pregnancy was getting close. I had been working up to this point, so, as a result of these changes, we decided that it would be better if I stopped working as a precautionary measure.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was given steroids to help mature the baby's lungs, as it was expected that the delivery would take place quite soon. The steroid was administered by an injection and I was given a further dose of steroids around 24 hours later. I was now being monitored twice weekly.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On Friday, 5 June 2015, it was found that my blood pressure had raised a little. I underwent a blood test to check my liver
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: function, and although it wasn't too bad, it had always been normal and it wasn't anymore.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Mr McCormack, the consultant, was on holiday. So Sara Brigham saw me and she admitted me to hospital that day as a safety precaution as she felt I would give birth in the next few days and she wanted me to be in a position where I could be closely monitored. I went home with my mum, packed some clothes and returned to the Countess as advised.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "That night, when being monitored, it was found that [Baby C]'s heart rate had dropped at around 2 in the morning. I was moved down to the labour ward because concerns had grown and it was felt that I may need to deliver my baby. On this occasion nothing happened. So in the morning I was moved back to the antenatal ward.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I continued to be to monitored over the weekend.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On Monday, 8 June 2015 Mr McCormack visited me and told me he would have delivered my baby on 15 June had he been present, but now he felt, looking at the current monitoring, it would be best to carry on with close monitoring. He told me that if my condition returned to how things were on the Friday, then the baby should be delivered.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The monitoring continued on the 8th and the 9th and then, on Wednesday 10 June, I went for a scan early in the morning. Mr McCormack performed my scan and told me there was no blood flow through the cord, and in fact it had started to reverse, which is a critical sign that you could be in danger of having a stillborn baby and the baby needed to be delivered that day.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I phoned [Father of Baby C] to arrange for him to come to the hospital before I was taken to the labour ward.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I was on the ward for most of the day and was given various drugs which helped to support the baby. One was magnesium sulphate, which matures the baby's brain.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Somewhere between 15.00 and 15.30 hours I was taken to theatre where Ms Rowe(?), an obstetrician, conducted a caesarean section procedure and delivered our baby, [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The birth was extremely stressful. There were several paediatric personnel within the theatre.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby C] was taken to the Resuscitaire on delivery in order to take care of him because he was so small and fragile. Sally [which is one of the doctors] came and told me she had intubated
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: him and placed him on a ventilator, but at that time they weren't necessarily concerned for him.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was treated and returned to the post-natal ward.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I wasn't able to visit [Baby C] for a number of hours as I needed to be able to stand without assistance. Being able to stand unaided was also hindered by the fact that I had been given a spinal anaesthetic as part of the caesarean.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I estimate it to have been around 8 or 9 o'clock on 10 June when I went down to see [Baby C]. He was now in nursery 1. He was tiny. He only weighed 800 grams.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "By the time I went to see [Baby C], the hospital staff had already taken him off the ventilator. He was given alternative breathing support in the form of continuous positive airway pressure, CPAP."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: It then continues to describe the events and says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "For the first time on 11 June, which was a Thursday, [Father of Baby C] and I had small periods of time where we could hold [Baby C]. I would say the neonatal nurse who was on most of the time was Jo [that is Joanne, Williams]. She was very supportive and reassuring and was able to answer all of our questions.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Friday 12 June was much the same. The only consultant we had any dealings with was John Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The following day, Saturday, 13 June, [Father of Baby C] and I spent all day on the neonatal unit. They had taken [Baby C] off the CPAP and put him on a very light flow of oxygen. [Baby C] did appear to be a lot calmer, having been a little agitated the day before. [Baby C] had a gastric tube fitted which went into his stomach.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: When they drew fluid from his stomach, I recall it being a black colour. They were unable to explain why this was, and as far as I am aware, it wasn't queried with the Liverpool Women's Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The staff remained positive with [Baby C]'s progress.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Father of Baby C] and I also had a cautious positivity. We weren't being unrealistic, but we could see he was doing all that could be expected of him, and his oxygen levels were being weaned down because he was doing so well.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That really was the state of play for the 13th.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was last on the neonatal unit around 10.30 that night when I had taken some milk down. There was a nurse on the unit looking after him that I had not seen before. She had dark hair and I felt she was a little abrupt with me, and after this I didn't see her again.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Initially, when [Baby C] was placed in nursery 1, there were other babies with him. Now, on Saturday the 13th, he was the only baby there.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Having gone to bed, I was awoken at 23.20 hours by one of the midwives from the post-natal ward. She had been contacted by one of the neonatal nurses who were requesting that I went to see [Baby C] urgently. She wouldn't tell me why.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I ran down to the neonatal unit where I could see CPR was being performed on [Baby C]. It was explained to me that his heart rate had suddenly dropped and he had stopped breathing without any warning. This had been very sudden and unexpected. They had given him a small amount of milk for the first time just a few minutes after, but they didn't think that was relevant. There were several people present, with at least two or three doctors and several nurses.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I contacted [Father of Baby C], who was at home in bed, and I told him what had happened, and that he needed to come to the hospital urgently.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Initially I didn't really take in what was happening and I didn't take in the severity, until I was asked by a neonatal nurse, somewhat unexpectedly, whether I wanted someone to call a priest. I remember feeling quite shocked and I asked her if she thought he was going to die, to which she responded, 'Yes, I think so'. This was a nurse I had never met before and I was surprised that this piece of information and communication came from a nurse rather than a doctor.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I am unsure whether she did this on the direction of a doctor or not.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The nurse did not tell me her name. She was in her mid to late 20s with a fair complexion and brown hair tied back in a ponytail.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I had to make a decision about calling the priest in the absence of my husband, who had not yet arrived.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Both Roman Catholic and Church of England priests were contacted in order for [Baby C] to be baptised. I had assumed [Baby C] could be baptised by both denominations and had been reassured by the nurse that it was fine to have both. It transpired, once
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: he had been baptised, he could not then be baptised again into another denomination.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Whilst waiting for the priest, [Father of Baby C] arrived on the unit. It seemed to take forever for the priest to arrive and all the time we were waiting CPR was being carried out on [Baby C]. We had to wait for around 50 minutes. If I had known it was going to take that long, I wouldn't have prolonged things. I just felt this was my only opportunity to have [Baby C] baptised.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I didn't want to regret not having done it at a later date. It was a way in which we were able to validity that he had been here. We wouldn't have anything else.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby C] was baptised by a Church of England priest.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "After the baptism, [Baby C] was handed to me and I was told he had passed away. I was holding him and he was still breathing. It was awful. I was telling them, 'He's breathing, he's got a pulse, he's not dead'.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: John Gibbs said to me, 'What would you like us to do?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you want us to carry on?' I said, 'No, I just want us to be together.' He wasn't the same baby now.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "In amongst all of this, they had scanned his brain and it was evident there had been extensive changes as he had been deprived of oxygen for quite a long period of time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I'm not sure what the time was. I went to [Baby C] at about 23.20 hours. The CPR and baptism went on for about an hour, so it was probably about half past midnight when we called our parents. Both mine and [Father of Baby C]'s parents came to the hospital, and we went into the lounge at the back of the neonatal unit where we just held [Baby C]. [Baby C] was given some morphine for comfort and he was much more settled with this:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "There were two neonatal nurses that were with us throughout this time. One of them was the nurse who had asked me earlier whether I wanted them to call the priest. The other I have no prior recollection of but I think her first name was Mel. These two nurses attended to us for the remainder of our time there.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: They came back to check on our welfare and they also took [Baby C]'s foot and handprints for us to keep. They asked if we wanted a lock of his hair and one of the two nurses took this for us. I cannot remember which nurse this was.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Shortly before he passed away, [Baby C] was given another dose of morphine by one of the nurses. Again, [Father of Baby C] can't recall which. This was around 05.30 hours on Sunday the 14th."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Moving on to the next day:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On Thursday, 15 June, I was contacted by either Alder Hey Children's Hospital or the coroner's office.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I was told [Baby C] had been transferred to Alder Hey and they were going to conduct a post-mortem there. I was contacted again later that day to say the post-mortem had now concluded and I should register [Baby C]'s death as natural causes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was told they were still awaiting the results of further tests for a more thorough conclusion, but that could take a few months. [Father of Baby C] and I were then able to arrange [Baby C]'s funeral. We had [Baby C] cremated at Blacon Crematorium."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That concludes the relevant part of [Mother of Baby C]'s statement.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of [Father of Baby C] (read)

Moving to a statement of her husband, [Father of Baby C], dated 10 December 2019, he identifies himself and states that he married [Mother of Baby C] on 31 May 2013, and that his wife became pregnant in early December 2014.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: He states that:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[He] would describe [Mother of Baby C]'s pregnancy as highly stressful. [He] is not aware of the names of any of the medication or medical procedures she had had to take, leading up to our baby's birth, but I do remember that she had to check her blood pressure on a regular basis.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Some time before our baby was born [he is not certain on the exact day, but 1 to 2 weeks before [Baby C] was born], [Mother of Baby C]'s blood pressure had increased. As this was one of the symptoms she had been asked to look out for, she attended the Countess hospital so she could be regularly monitored. They admitted her as a safety precaution. I cannot remember exact details of how I was informed. I think [Mother of Baby C] was admitted to hospital following a scan. She stayed at the hospital and was monitored.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The elective section was planned for the morning of 10 June 2015. On my arrival to the hospital I met up with [Mother of
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Baby C] and we were briefed by her consultant, Mr Jim McCormack, and approximately four to five other people.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We were then led into the operating room and our son, [Baby C], was born by caesarean section shortly afterwards. After being born he was wrapped up and placed into an incubator. I remember the medical staff being really pleased with him as he was displaying positive signs that he was going to be okay. [Baby C] was then taken to the neonatal ward while [Mother of Baby C] was taken to a separate ward to recover.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I followed [Baby C] to the neonatal ward, which I would describe as a secure ward within the Countess hospital. To gain access you have to be buzzed in by an intercom system. Once inside, there's a corridor with rooms off. I was directed to a glass-fronted large room on the left. This room was able to accommodate other babies but I can't remember if there were other babies present at this time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remained with [Baby C], and [Mother of Baby C] joined us a few hours later. He was still doing well. For the majority of time he needed to use a respirator whilst he was in his incubator, but this wasn't all of the time. [Baby C] would fight with the tubes and face mask. He was capable of breathing independently. Staff continued to monitor his progress. At no time did they express any concern of him not surviving.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby C] was cared for by a number of nurses whilst at the Countess of Chester Hospital. As I was generally only there during the day, leaving around 7 to 8 pm each evening, I can only recall one specific nurse. I cannot recall the name, which cared for him during the day shifts. I would describe her as Nurse 1."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And he gives this general description:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "White with blonde/brown hair which was tied up in a ponytail, aged mid 20s. She had a mild manner, 5 foot 6 inches tall, slender build. I cannot her name.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I think she was wearing scrubs most of the time, but I cannot be certain.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As with any premature baby, [Baby C] was not fed initially with any milk as they were monitoring his bowel function, which appeared to be working okay as he was able to pass urine and small poos. On the 11th and 12 June, [Mother of Baby C] and I took turns in holding him.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 13 June 2015 I spent the day with [Mother of Baby C] and [Baby C] on the ward. I think this was the day [Baby C] had his
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: first milk feed. As far as I am aware, no problems arose from this feed and he continued to progress well and staff remained positive. He was still in an incubator and receiving care by staff. Some time early evening, around 7 pm, I left the ward and went home.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Later that evening I was awoken by my mobile ringing. It was [Mother of Baby C]. She told me that I had to get to the hospital right away, so I grabbed some clothes and immediately made my way.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As I approached the neonatal ward, [Mother of Baby C] was waiting for me in the corridor. She told me that [Baby C] had collapsed and had stopped breathing. She'd also agreed for a priest to come so that [Baby C] could be baptised as they didn't believe he was going to make it.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: We walked into the ward together and entered [Baby C]'s room, which was the same one he'd always been in.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby C] was lying in his incubator. A plastic casing which that normally encased it had been removed and a red-haired female -- I'm not sure whether she was a nurse a doctor or a midwife. This female, who I had not seen before, was attempting to resuscitate him by performing CPR. Also present was a male consultant.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The red-haired female, who I will refer to for the purposes of this statement as Nurse 2, attempted to resuscitate [Baby C] for a long time. At one point she turned to the consultant present and said she didn't think she could do anymore. However, she kept going whilst we waited for the priest. Once [Baby C] was baptised, they stopped trying to resuscitate him. It was during that time that [Baby C] started breathing on his own.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Mother of Baby C] and [I] were escorted into a family room by two further nurses who I will refer to as Nurses 3 and 4.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: There were more people around but I can't picture them.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: This included the priest.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Nurse 3 I describe as a white female with long mousy-brown hair which had been tied up, slim to medium build, aged around mid 20s. I have seen this nurse's picture in the newspaper after her arrest and I now know her name to be Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Nurse 4 was also a white female with light brown shoulder length hair, slender build, aged late 20s to early 30s.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Whilst in this room, [Mother of Baby C] and I took turns holding him as we knew he wasn't going to make it. We just wanted to spend this time together. We'd also called our parents who attended. The priest left shortly after [Mother of Baby C]'s parents' arrival.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember during this time one of the nurses administered some morphine. I think this happened on more than one occasion, possibly two to three times.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At regular intervals Nurses 3 and 4 came in to check on our welfare. They also took [Baby C]'s hand and footprints for us to keep. Clothes and toys from his cot were also gathered and given to us. There was nothing else that could be done for [Baby C]. It was just a matter of time before he would die, so we just wanted to cuddle him and make sure he was pain-free until that time came.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember at one point one of the nurses -- I think it could have been Nurse 3, but I'm not 100% sure -- came in with a ventilated basket. She turned to us and said words similar to, 'You have said your goodbyes now, do you want me to put him in here?' referring to the basket. This comment shook us. [Mother of Baby C] said, 'He's not died yet'. The nurse then attempted to backtrack and defuse the situation, but I couldn't believe what she'd said. We didn't want to leave him when he was still alive.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When [Baby C] sadly died it was around 5 am on 14 June. [Baby C] was put in a ventilated basket before being moved to the room next door where we were escorted by either Nurse 3 or 4. Once inside we placed the basket on the floor and said our goodbyes before shutting the door and leaving him. [Mother of Baby C] then went back to the maternity ward to collect her belongings and to say goodbye to the staff there."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER
